policies.summary: A solar development approved under the Site Location of Development Act on high-value agricultural land must pay a compensation fee based on the affected area (reducible for dual-use agrivoltaics) or permanently conserve an equal area of farmland.

Wind and solar developments that meet the Site Location of Development Act size triggers (more than 20 acres, or buildings, roads, paved areas and stripped or graded areas not revegetated covering more than 3 acres) need Department of Environmental Protection approval before construction. The Department is the defined primary siting authority under the Wind Energy Act only for expedited wind energy developments, meaning grid-scale wind in the expedited permitting area (all organized areas plus places in unorganized areas named by Land Use Planning Commission rule). Municipalities also regulate through their own ordinances.

No state agency or municipality may license, permit, lease or grant rights for an offshore wind turbine in state-owned submerged lands or territorial waters, except small short-term research turbines, the designated research array project, and port facilities or cables serving wind projects in federal waters.
State rule limits sound from routine operation of grid-scale and small-scale wind developments to 55 dBA by day and 42 dBA at night at protected locations, and 75 dBA at the project property line.

Active as of 2026-09-23 per the carina.energy BESS tracker (expiring June 2026 at last check). Adopted 2024-11-25 for an initial 180-day term and repeatedly extended by Select Board vote. Legal basis: Moratorium Ordinance on Grid-Level Battery Energy Storage Systems, Grid-Level Substations and Grid-Scale Wind Energy Projects.

Battery energy storage system regulation (proposed, covering all BESS). Pending as of 2026-09-23 per the carina.energy BESS tracker; a proposed moratorium that would cover all battery storage (not just utility-scale), which would make it one of few ALL_BESS-scope moratoria outside New York. Not confirmed adopted; town's own warrant article/ordinance text not located within the research budget. Preemptive; the town cited the absence of specific data center standards in its Land Use Ordinance/Comprehensive Plan, the experience of Wiscasset and Lewiston with inadequate regulatory frameworks, and a desire to protect the Georges River watershed and electrical infrastructure. Active as of 2026-09-23. Voters approved the moratorium in near-unanimous fashion (per SAVRN, roughly 60 residents attended, nearly double normal turnout) at a special town meeting on 2026-07-08, prohibiting Data Center and Data Center Accessory Use (including battery energy storage systems as an accessory use) townwide for 180 days from enactment, renewable in further 180-day increments. No data center applications had been filed in Warren. Legal basis: Town of Warren Moratorium on Data Center and Data Center Accessory Development, adopted by special town meeting vote 2026-07-08 pursuant to 30-A M.R.S.A. § 4356.

In August 2021, after residents voiced aesthetic concerns about utility-scale solar projects, the City Council imposed a moratorium for up to 180 days on solar projects.
In August 2023, the Brewer city council adopted a 6-month moratorium on large-scale solar projects.
Residents voted to adopt a new ordinance requiring solar projects to be set back 300 feet and impose a moratorium on utility lines.
In March 2024, the Town of Athens passed a 180-day moratorium on large-scale solar facilities, citing the potential for water contamination, as well as wildlife concerns.
A moratorium on wind and solar projects that went into effect August 2020 was extended multiple times as the town developed new ordinances for wind and solar energy.
In February 2024, the Town of Cutler imposed a moratorium on solar facilities, citing additional time to draft amendments to its Land Use Ordinance to accommodate solar facilities.
Town Council passed a 180-day moratorium on commercial solar arrays.

As of November 2017, the Wind Energy Facility Ordinance for the Town of Dixfield requires that wind turbines be set back 4,000 feet from any occupied building and 2,000 feet from the boundaries of the project parcel unless the developer secures a waiver from the pertinent abutting landowner and technical evidence of the soundness of any reduced setback.
In November 2015, the Town of Freedom enacted a wind turbine ordinance that requires all wind turbines be set back 2,500 feet from any Scenic or Special Resource.
In April 2021, the Town of Glenburn imposed a 2-month moratorium on commercial solar facilities.
In November 2024, the Town of Greene voted overwhelmingly to adopt an amendment limiting the size of any solar project to 15 acres.

The town’s zoning ordinance provides that wind turbines must be set back at least 1 mile from property lines of nonparticipating residences or 13 times the height of the turbine, whichever is greater.
In November 2023, Moscow residents voted to ban commercial wind farms in the municipality.
In March 2022, voters at the annual Smithfield Town Meeting approved a 180-day moratorium on commercial solar development.
In November 2023, the Town of Moscow voted to ban commercial solar farms in the municipality.
The Town of Dixmont’s Wind Energy Facility Ordinance requires that wind energy facilities be set back 2,500 feet from the property line of nonparticipating residences.
On October 14, 2021, Dixmont adopted a 180-day moratorium on solar arrays.
The Town of Woodstock’s Commercial Wind Energy Facility Ordinance establishes setback requirements of 1 mile from non-participating property lines and 3,000 feet from scenic or special resources.
In February 2022, Otisfield residents voted to establish a 6-month moratorium on commercial solar facilities, which was extended several times.
In January 2022, Lovell residents voted to approve a 180 moratorium on large-scale solar projects.
In September 2016, the Rome Selectboard approved the request of the Rome Planning Board to extend a wind energy moratorium for another 180 days in order to develop a wind energy ordinance.
In 2023, the Town of Trenton’s Select Board passed a moratorium on large-scale Solar Projects in response to a proposed 70-MW solar farm.
In July 2024, the Select Board of the Town of Penobscot approved a 180-day moratorium on solar projects larger than 20 kW.
In June 2023, the Select Board approved a 6-month moratorium on commercial solar energy facilities, citing a need for more time to draft ordinances regulating solar facilities.
In September 2015, the Fort Fairfield Town Council passed a wind ordinance requiring a 1-mile setback from all non-participating properties.
In April 2024, the Town of Turner passed a zoning ordinance that required solar farms to include a vegetated buffer of at least 50 feet in depth to mitigate the visual impact.

projects.description: The Aroostook Renewable Gateway Project is a 150-mile, 1,200-MW transmission corridor designed to transmit energy from the proposed 170-turbine King Pine Wind Farm in Aroostook County to consumers in southern Maine and Massachusetts.
An anti-wind group called Friends of Maine’s Mountains filed a lawsuit against developer SunEdison to stop construction of the 185-MW Bingham Wind project.
In December 2015, the Maine Supreme Judicial Court affirmed the ruling of the Maine Board of Environmental Protection that rejected SunEdison’s permit for the $100 million Bowers Mountain Wind Farm.

In 2011, the local organization Concerned Citizens of Rural Hancock County (CCRHC) intervened in a public evidentiary hearing before the Land Use Regulation Commission (LURC) to challenge developer Blue Sky East, LLC’s request for a permit to build the 19-turbine, 34-MW Bull Hill Wind Project.
In April 2010, a group of neighbors organized as the Fox Islands Wind Neighbors began complaining about noise from the recently completed 4.5-MW Fox Islands Wind project.
At a town meeting on June 18, 2022, residents of Greene voted overwhelmingly against a proposal to lease 80 acres of public land to Greene Apple Solar Power as part of a 600-acre, 120-MW solar farm.

In 2012, Friends of the Boundary Mountains filed a lawsuit in federal court challenging the Army Corps of Engineers’ issuance of a Clean Water Act permit to allow for the installation of a 15-turbine, 45-MW project adjacent to an existing 132-MW project.

The Maine Supreme Judicial Court dismissed a nuisance lawsuit in 2013 against a wind energy company over its northern Maine wind farm, which the plaintiff argued created a noise so loud he was forced to sleep in a soundproof bunker in his garage.
In December 2020, the Monmouth Select Board voted to place a retroactive solar energy moratorium on the ballot for a vote by town residents.
An 11-MW demonstration offshore wind farm to test the feasibility of floating wind turbines was preliminarily approved by the Maine Public Utilities Commission (PUC) in 2014.
In 2017, Central Maine Power, a subsidiary of Avangrid, proposed the New England Clean Energy Connect (NECEC).

In 2010, the Martha A. Powers Trust filed a lawsuit against the Maine Board of Environmental Protection alleging that the Board erred in finding that noise from the 48-turbine, 150-MW Oakfield Wind project would not generate unreasonable adverse health effects.
In March 2012, Passadumkeag Windpark LLC, a subsidiary of Quantum Utility Generation, submitted a permit application for the construction of the 14-turbine, 42-MW Passadumkeag wind farm.
A 7-acre, 1-MW solar farm proposed by Allen Solar is facing resistance from the town of Raymond.

In 2012, the organization Friends of Maine Mountains (“Friends”) filed an appeal with the Maine Supreme Judicial Court challenging the state Board of Environmental Protection (BEP)’s February 18, 2012 final order approving the 34-MW Saddleback Ridge Wind Project.

In 2017, local residents, including groups called Saving Maine and the Moosehead Region Futures Committee, organized in opposition to NRG’s proposed 26-turbine, 94-MW Somerset Wind project in Somerset County, Maine.
